questions.topic: UAE gold counted up to three times
questions.answer: No triple count in the central values. UAE customs record gold by the country it was shipped from, so Armenian-routed Russian gold sits under Armenia, not Russia, in UAE imports (2023: 40.9 t / USD 2.58bn from Armenia beside 40.6 t / USD 2.52bn from Russia; Swissaid 2024: 66 t from Russia and 78 t from Armenia listed separately). Hong Kong does the same (2023: 7.8 t from Armenia, matching Armenia's 7.4 t to Hong Kong). Hidden UAE gold is zero in 2022-2025. Two real problems remain: (a) the Armenian-routed gold (EUR 7.6bn central 2022-26) is kept in full by the UAE, while the UAE passes on 84-91% of its direct Russian gold; it should be passed on the same way; (b) hidden UAE gold 2026 (central EUR 1.8bn) rests on the same argument that was dropped for 2024-2025, and Russian gold moved to Hong Kong in 2025-26.

questions.topic: Russian crude and fuel delivered to the UAE
questions.answer: Counted nowhere. CREA has Russian fuel discharged in the UAE worth EUR 0.81bn (2021), 5.62 (2022), 6.05 (2023), 2.14 (2024), 1.60 (2025), 0.19 (2026), almost all products; UAE customs record only EUR 0.07, 0.27 and 1.07bn of HS 27 from Russia in 2021-2023. `laundered` holds fuel refined from Russian crude elsewhere (India) and does not contain this; the max(customs, fossil) rule only runs for pipeline-gas countries; hub resale only moves `laundered`. Missing: EUR 13.3bn (2022-26). Net of resale (UAE resale share 0.30/0.42/0.65 from UAE re-export records; bunkers stay with the hub, as the method does elsewhere) the UAE keeps EUR 8.1bn (3.9-11.6); EUR 5.6bn is resold, of which EUR 4.7bn to named customers (low 0, because buyers that record origin may already hold it; highs per buyer are not additive). The 2021 level (EUR 0.74bn missing) is added to the UAE baseline at 2019-2021 prices.

questions.answer: Germany: no overlap. Kiel's tracker (Release 31) allocates EUR 25.0bn of military aid; Kiel's own October 2026 brief traces EUR 22.7bn of budget military aid for 2022-25 and EUR 11.6bn appropriated for 2026, but keeps those budget figures out of the tracker because disbursement is unknown. The map's EUR 1.8bn (0.3 in 2025, 1.5 in 2026) sits on top of the tracker and well below Kiel's budget-based figure (gap up to about EUR 9bn): keep it. France: overlap. The 2022-23 part (EUR 1.0bn) is the gap between Kiel's price-list valuation and France's official EUR 2.6bn, but Kiel adopted the official EUR 2.6bn as its allocation from Release 16 (April 2024), so Release 31 already contains it. The 2024 part should also lose the EUR 0.3bn financed from frozen Russian assets (the map leaves Russia's money out elsewhere). Corrected France: 2022 0 (0-0.3), 2023 0 (0-0.3), 2024 0.7 (0-1.7), 2025 0.2 (0-1.0), 2026 0.1 (0-0.5): total 1.0 (0-3.8) instead of 2.3 (0.3-5.5).
questions.certainty: A that Kiel uses France's official figure (Kiel's own note); C for the 2024 split

questions.topic: China's sales to Russia: hub re-exports against the residual import gap
questions.answer: The two modules do not overlap in their central values: re-exports move value that hubs record in their own exports to Russia, capped by their recorded imports, while the transit part of the residual is goods partners report as sold to Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan that those hubs never record as imports. They overlap only at the high end, where the import cap is dropped (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan highs). The real problem is elsewhere: Russia's imports exceeded partner exports by 6.5-9.2% of its imports before the war (partner/FCS ratio 0.908-0.935), of which freight is 3.5-7.5%; the remaining structural gap (about EUR 6bn a year) is inside the pro-rata 'residual' component that is added to 2022-2026 sales but never to the 2019-2021 baseline. It is allocated by reported exports with weight 1 for non-coalition countries, so China gets about half. Removing it from 2022-2026 (EUR 5.6/6.9/6.5/5.7/3.8bn, plus or minus 3.5bn a year) cuts China's sales to Russia by EUR 17.2bn (7.4-27.0) nominal.

effect_eur_bn.nominal: all countries -28.5 (-44.8 to -12.2) for 2022-26, of which China -17.2, Kazakhstan -2.1, Turkey -1.5

questions.also_noted: Belarus's share of the residual (EUR 9bn 2022-25) disappears when narrow.json replaces Belarus's sales with official totals; that part of Russia's import gap is now assigned to nobody (an under-count, not a double count).
questions.certainty: B that the structural gap is missing from the baseline (method), C for its size

KAZ.drivers: Less paid to Russia 13.9 and less paid for services 3.3. Imports from Russia rose in money terms (EUR 14.1bn 2021 to 16.1bn 2025), but the counterfactual grows 9.4% a year (multiplier 1.39 by 2026), fitted on 2016-2021 only: the rebound from the 2014-16 tenge collapse. The full 2012-2021 window gives +0.8% a year. Sales to Russia have the same issue (+9.6% against +0.2%).

CYP.drivers: Services sold to Russia given up 9.2: Cyprus's own BoP shows EUR 2.2-2.3bn a year before the war (business and financial services to Russian-owned holdings, ship management, tourism) and 0.5bn since 2023, after EU bans on accounting, consulting and trust services.
CYP.verdict: real fall (A-grade data), but counted at gross revenue; much of it was income from Russian capital booked in Cyprus that moved to the UAE and elsewhere. At the 20% profit share used for costs it would be about EUR 1.8bn (about 9% of GDP in total). No data correction proposed; a method choice to flag.

MNE.drivers: Services given up 0.79 and refugees 0.26. Montenegro's services sold to Russia rose (EUR 0.16bn 2019-21 average, 0.35bn 2023, 0.26bn 2024), but the counterfactual applies a COVID rebound of x1.8 to x2.8 (unreliable trend) to the 2019-2021 average, putting expected sales at EUR 0.46bn a year, far above the 2019 peak of about 0.30bn.
MNE.verdict: artefact: cap the counterfactual at the 2019 level

MRT.drivers: Less paid 0.45 and sales given up 0.42 on a GDP of EUR 10bn. Mauritania recorded USD 0.12-0.13bn a year of Russian-origin fuel in 2019-2020, while Russia recorded only USD 1-2m of fuel exports to Mauritania: traders' cargoes labelled by origin. From 2022 the fuel arrives via the UAE, Togo and India and is no longer labelled Russian. Fish exports to Russia (USD 0.05-0.10bn) did stop.
MRT.verdict: mostly artefact (relabelled fuel); the fish sales are real but small. The baseline's low end is negative (a linear 2019-2021 trend run below zero), a builder bug.

LBN.drivers: Less paid 1.9: the 2019-2021 baseline includes 2019 (USD 1.2bn, before Lebanon's financial collapse cut imports by about 40%); with the 2020-2021 average the part falls to about 0.9. Purchases from Ukraine +0.6 and laundered oil -0.6.
LBN.verdict: mostly artefact of a pre-war baseline set before an unrelated economic collapse; real shift at most EUR 0.5-1bn (2-4% of GDP)

LTU.drivers: Less paid 14.9 (pre-war Russian crude for the Mazeikiai refinery, 56% of imports, about 70% of whose output was exported) and sales given up 12.7 (85-90% of Lithuania's pre-war exports to Russia were re-exports of goods made elsewhere).
LTU.verdict: partly artefact: re-exports and processing trade counted as Lithuanian money. After Q6 31% (24% if refinery exports are also taken out); still high because every euro of lost trade counts in full.

EST.drivers: Less paid 5.8 (Russian oil products entrepot through Muuga, a quarter of pre-war imports re-exported), sales given up 1.9 (35-41% re-exports), services 3.0.

questions.general: Trend windows fitted on 2016-2021 only are used as 'reliable' in 68 series. Where the 2012-13 level lies well above the post-2016 line, the fit is a rebound from the 2014-16 crash. Replacing the rate with the full-window rate moves China by -35.7, Kazakhstan by -21.7, Belarus by -5.6, Uzbekistan by -2.4 and Kyrgyzstan by -1.4 (EUR bn, toward Russia).
questions.certainty: B for the diagnosis (data and fit notes), C for the replacement trends

questions.topic: Pre-war transit and re-exports in Baltic and Finnish imports from Russia
questions.method: Imports from Russia by heading (UN Comtrade, 2019-2021) are split into gas (left out: the map already swaps it for final-use gas), goods passed on unprocessed and goods processed and exported. Estonia's HS 27 entrepot share comes from customs tonnes against Eurostat energy-balance imports from Russia (energy statistics exclude transit) and from Estonia's own HS 27 re-export records; Latvian steel from its export/import ratio with no steel mill since 2016; refinery export shares from Eurostat product exports against crude and product imports.
questions.recommendation: Remove the 'strict' share from the 2019-2021 baseline and from the yearly values (central EST 0.26, LVA 0.27, LTU 0.075, FIN 0.014) and give it to the final buyers. The 'processed_extra' share (LTU 0.39, FIN 0.32: refinery crude and Finnish nickel matte) should be treated like Turkey's and India's exported crude only if pre-war laundered oil also gets a baseline; otherwise keep it with the refiner.

sold_side.note: Not asked, but larger: the same countries' pre-war sales to Russia were largely re-exports, which the hub re-export module does not cover for EU members. Share of exports to Russia: LTU 0.80/0.85/0.90 (85% in 2013; under 2.5% of Lithuanian output went to Russia in 2017), EST 0.35/0.39/0.45 (Estonia's own re-export records), LVA 0.30/0.45/0.60 (assumed, no origin split published), FIN 0.05/0.10/0.20 (assumed). Moved to EU makers by their own sales to Russia, keeping a 7% margin.

questions.answer: The 5.5% cut should skip pipeline gas valued at the border (final-use gas at own contract prices), pipeline crude (Druzhba, ESPO), electricity, and trade over land with neighbours, where the freight up to the border is paid to Russian pipelines and railways. LNG and seaborne crude keep the cut. Border-priced share of to_rus (central, 2019-2021 then 2022-2026): Hungary 0.86 then 0.96-1.0, Slovakia 0.83 then 0.85-1.0, Czechia 0.73 then 0.89 falling to 0, Austria 0.63 then 0.84-0.88 to 2024, Germany 0.58 then 0.63 (2022) and 0, Italy 0.48 then 0.21-0.62, Poland 0.42 then 0.41 (2022), China 0.45 (ESPO and Power of Siberia pipelines, rail), Serbia, North Macedonia, Bosnia 0.26-0.59 rising to 0.6-1.0 (TurkStream). Countries in narrow.json (Belarus, Kazakhstan, Turkey, UAE and others) already skip the cut because narrow values overwrite it. Ranges are plus or minus 0.1.
questions.certainty: C (pipeline volumes rounded; overland shares for China, Azerbaijan, Moldova, Tajikistan and the Baltics are estimates)

other_issues.issue: narrow.json overwrites to_rus/from_rus after the freight cut, re-exports and residual have run
other_issues.detail: The UAE, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Uzbekistan and others hold frozen copies of an earlier builder output (re-export moves, freight cut and residual included), so later changes upstream (refine.json shares, freight) no longer reach them; Belarus's official values are not cut for freight at all.
EUR 9bn of Russia's 2022-25 import gap allocated to Belarus vanishes when narrow.json replaces Belarus's sales; it should be re-spread or the residual recomputed with the official Belarus figures.
trade_full's linear trend_2022 can go below zero (Mauritania sales to Russia: base_range low -0.007); floor alternative baselines at 0.

other_issues.issue: Laundered oil has no pre-war baseline
other_issues.detail: neg(sum(laundered)) counts all fuel made from Russian crude as new since 2022, although refiners in Lithuania, Finland, Belarus, India and Turkey exported such fuel before the war; this inflates payments to Russia for the fuel buyers and blocks a consistent treatment of Baltic and Finnish refinery exports (Q6).

other_issues.issue: Lost trade counted at gross value in the shift
other_issues.detail: Sales given up (goods and services) count in full in the shift, but at 20% in the cost. For service-heavy or re-export economies (Cyprus 9.2, Lithuania 12.7 before Q6) this dominates the headline. A margin-based shift would be the defensible headline; the current one should at least be labelled as turnover.
Official UAE-Russia non-oil trade USD 20.4bn in 2025 against about USD 12bn in the map; the 2025 trade layer is an IMF estimate.
2019 import level precedes the 2019-20 financial collapse; a 2020-2021 baseline (or a GDP-scaled one) halves 'less paid'.
